Target Email: mburke@pogustgoodhead.com
Aliases: MB, Michael, Michael B., M. Burke

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. TARGETED THREAD ANALYSIS: Focus your analysis primarily on the MOST RECENT (top-level) email AND the IMMEDIATELY FORWARDED/REPLIED-TO email (the second email in the chain).
2. "KEEP" DECISION: You MUST return "keep" ONLY IF the Data Subject:
   - Is a Sender, Recipient, CC, or BCC of the top-level email OR the immediately forwarded/replied-to email.
   - Is explicitly discussed or mentioned by name in the newly written body text of the top-level email.
3. IMMEDIATE FORWARD/REPLY CONTEXT: If the Data Subject is the sender/recipient of a message that was forwarded by someone else to a third-party, you MUST keep both the original message AND the forwarded message.
   - Case Study: John (Subject) sends an email to Jane. Jane forwards John's email to Pedro. Pedro replies to Jane adding Sandra.
   - Analysis: In this scenario, keep the original message John sent to Jane, and the email Jane forwarded to Pedro (as it contains the direct communication from the Subject). Discard subsequent emails where the Subject's message is no longer actively discussed.
   - Chronological Order Warning: Outlook puts newer messages first. This means the Subject's original forwarded message will appear near the bottom of the raw text block. Scan the entire document carefully to locate it.

5. NESTED EMAIL ATTACHMENTS (RECURSIVE CARRIERS): If the top-level email is unrelated but contains an attached email (.eml/.msg file) that matches the KEEP criteria, you MUST mark both the attached email AND the parent carrier email as "keep".
   - Case Study: Anne sends an email to Bob. Anne's email contains an attached email from the Subject to Carlos.
   - Analysis: Keep the attached email because the Subject is a participant. Keep Anne's email because it is the physical carrier of the attachment and must be preserved to allow extraction.
6. OUTPUT FORMAT: You must return ONLY a raw JSON object. Do not wrap the output in markdown code blocks (```json). Do not add conversational text.
Format exactly like this: {"decision": "keep" | "discard", "reason": "Brief justification."}

From: Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>
Sent: Thursday, October 9, 2025 11:07 AM
To: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>; Adam Solomon (UK) <Adam.Solomon@virginmediao2.co.uk>; Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>; Dexter Baker (UK) <Dexter.Baker1@virginmediao2.co.uk>; Laura Coogan <laura.coogan@virginmediao2.co.uk>
Cc: Ford Litigation Team <fordteam@pogustgoodhead.com>; Priyanka Gladson <pgladson@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Re: The Ford NOx Emissions Group Litigation - Strictly Private and Confidential




Dear Adam,




Thank you again for taking the time to meet with us. It was a pleasure to connect.

As I explained, I appreciate that recent developments and press coverage may have raised some questions. Please rest assured that PG remains fully committed to advancing the Ford NOx litigation with strength and focus. We continue to represent the largest cohort
 of claimants, including approximately 50% of all Ford claimants, and our priority remains achieving a successful outcome on your behalf.

Our team remains highly resourced and experienced, with long-standing NOx team members actively leading the case, including preparations for the upcoming PDD trial. We were pleased with how the Judge engaged at the recent PTR and look forward to updating the Claimants’
 Committee in more detail shortly.

As you know there has been a recent change in team personnel, which is a natural part of the evolution of a long-running case. The team remains fully operational and focused, and the transition has been managed to ensure continuity. The Judge was informed and
 expressed confidence in the team’s ongoing work.

I’ve now taken on senior responsibility for the litigation, supported by Anna, who is also looking forward to meeting you. As I understand you are keen to connect, we’ll arrange an introductory call shortly. I’ll also ensure we have regular calls scheduled
 to keep you fully updated on developments in the coming weeks.

Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions as we’re fully committed to supporting you.

Kind regards, 



































​​​​



























Alicia Alinia













Chief Executive Officer













+44 (0) 7890 043 629

Unfortunately, I wont be able to make our 10.30 this morning. There are a few spill over matters from the PTR which the judge is hearing this morning and I need to be in attendance.

For my part, I am keen to re-arrange to meet you and your colleagues at another time and when convenient for you. 




Apologies again for missing our call and look forwarding to speaking soon.

I look forward to speaking.

Good morning Raminder,
 
I have now had a chance to look at this. My thoughts are below:-
 
General Advice
 
My advice is as follows:-
 

Clearly in a perfect world obtaining an employee’s consent/ buy in to any sort of change is always preferable – however in my view this is
not necessary here and I entirely understand and appreciate why we would not want to have to do this in any event;The reason why consent is
not necessary is:-


Clause 4.2(c) of their contracts of employment requires each of them during their employment to “comply with all reasonable and lawful directions given to the Employee
 by the Company” – in my view working with Martyn Day on ongoing litigation which they have been working hand in glove with him on anyway for several years for a trial that starts next week is a reasonable and lawful direction;Clause 4.2(b) of their contracts of employment requires each of them during their employment to “diligently
 exercise such powers and perform such duties as may from time to time be assigned to the Employee by the Company;” – this is the same point.Although my view is that Clauses 4.2 (b) and (c) adequately cover the point, there is an additional helpful provision at Clause 4.1 of their contracts which states “The
Employee shall serve the
Company as a
Senior Associate
and will report to
Legal Director or their nominee.” As such Martyn Day could be designated as the “nominee” for the purposes of their contracts.


Please note that there are additional relevant clauses in their contracts which they should be complying with e.g. “to
use
their
best endeavours
to promote,
protect, develop
and extend
the business of the Company.” Their actions are, in my view, in clear breach of this.Sarah Bingham’s reference to Clause 4.2(a) in her email is correct albeit she has spun the meaning for her own
 purposes – the business of the Company remains exactly as it was before and taking some direction from Martyn Day for the common good does not change that;The concept of working on a case with other individuals outside of the firm giving directions to them on a piece
 of litigation is hardly a novel concept – for example, presumably these individuals do work at the behest of external counsel? No consent is required for those arrangements.
 
Pallas’s Questions
 
Turning specifically to Pallas’s email of 8.39pm last evening and the relevant questions for us:-
 
3. I agree entirely with Pallas’s paragraph 3. If the employees were being seconded they would need to give specific consent but this is not a secondment and falls within the
 confines of their contracts of employment as explained above;
5.2. Given JLG and Gallagher’s behaviour to date, notwithstanding that Nick Johnson confirmed in writing to Alicia that he agreed to the case leads remaining employed by PG until
 the end of the trial, their ongoing behaviour suggests that they may still be manouevring to escape early. It is therefore essential that all communications with them continue the tone of Anna’s email to them of Saturday 4 October – i.e. respectful/ open to
 hearing their concerns (however ridiculous they may be) and avoiding any opportunity for them to argue that PG have somehow breached their contracts of employment. That is not to say that we cannot respectfully push back on their points. Pallas’s suggestion
 of a meeting is eminently sensible albeit that PG should bear in mind that the case leads may try and get a rise out of PG in that meeting on purpose to argue that there has been a break down in relations. On this point, given that the trial starts next week,

AA Agreement
 

I understand that the word “solely” has been removed from the document. This is helpful in that it deals with one of their points. It also reduces the scale of the delegation

not essential however for the purposes of this Agency agreement – it would be enough to tell the employees that Martyn is the person  - or one of the people - they need to report to;Otherwise I have no more comments on the Agency agreement.
 
I hope that this helps but if you or Pallas or anyone else have any queries please do not hesitate to ask.

a.     
We can’t totally ignore the case leads

b.     
Tell LD (and counsel) the AA can’t be finalised before the PTR

c.     
Speak to LD after the PTR to make necessary changes

The emails back and forth with this team is getting us nowhere. We think there needs to be a meeting with them, attended by Alicia and Anna.
 That obviously can’t be before the PTR, so would need to be on Tuesday at the earliest. But it might even have to be Wednesday. We would prepare you for this.Their overwhelming issue is the delegation of work by LD to individual solicitors at PG. This has always seemed problematic to us, but LD

To be clear, we are not conceding the principle that the case leads have the right to consent to this agreement – but they can’t just be
 ignored.


We consider (but should get it cleared by Clydes) that there is nothing inherently wrong or out of the ordinary with an employer telling
 an employee to do, for a limited period and for specific work, what a responsible third party tells it to do – as long as the employer continues to oversee and supervise (including in the SRA sense) the employee. So if the employer considers the employee is
 nor being directed properly, it can tell the employee not longer to follow the directions of the third party.But that situation is not precisely what we have, because of the word “solely” in the Agency Agreement, where it relates to LD’s supervision
 of PG personnel doing the Common Work delegated to them. That makes it appear that only LD will know what the PG employees will do, so PG can no longer supervise them.So what is the way forward? We suggest the following:

 During that discussion, give them a summary of the case leads’ concerns, remind them that they want and need to work with the case leads, and the only way we can see this getting anywhere is if we drop the word “solely”. We must also tell them that

 it should not be sent until we have reviewed it and determined if it should be sent, consistent with our strategy.

 their supervisors, and you can be super-robust about everything else.


We would also suggest that after that meeting, you have a follow-up with them and Martyn Day, but we have to make sure Martyn is on side

Dear Anna, 



Thank you for your email. 



We have some overarching points to raise before addressing the points in your email regarding the Side Letter Agency Agreement (“SL AA”). 



First and foremost, we have raised serious and significant issues regarding how traumatic we, and the entire team, are finding this process and that we have genuine concerns
 for the mental health and well-being of our staff. We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those concerns,
 nor does it even mention them. 



We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work and non-PDD
 Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything we
 have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on critical
 workstreams.  



Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions and, in aid
 of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness statements.
 You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board, despite Pogust
 Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that dismisses our concerns
 and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  



For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this has been put
 in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement either does
 not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted and the
 intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  



If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious engagement
 from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  



We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. 



On the points in your email: 


1.                  
Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter 


You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged”
within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding
 that the new arrangement is entirely novel.  



 



You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear that it goes
 further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects: 



 



a.
Formal separation of supervision and control 



The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG. Indeed, we
 understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx AA. That agreement
 permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations. 



 



b.
Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions 



The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy or reassign
 its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer. 



 



The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that “this will
 not practically change much day to day.”  



 


2.                  
Tension with Employment Contracts 


Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there will be no
 change to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. 



Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly conflicts
 with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract: 


 

a.
Duty of obedience and supervision 

Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to comply with
 PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD in respect
 of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract. 

 

b.
Regulatory oversight 

The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the supervising
 solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?  

 

These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.  

 

c. Consent and legal clarity 

The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains the employer,
 yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise. 


 


3.                  
Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk 
The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. If PG personnel are performing common
 work solely under LD’s direction (as the SL AA confirms), then it is not clear whose professional indemnity (“PI”) insurance would respond in the event of a professional error. This is in circumstances where PG remains the/our employer and is responsible
 for holding PI cover for its staff. But LD is envisaged as exercising the day to-day control and making the litigation decisions. The SRA expects supervision and insurance liability to be aligned. That is not the case here. 


 



This is not hypothetical. A clear example of this risk occurred this week when LD made a costs offer to the Mercedes Defendants without PG’s knowledge or approval from PG's
 insurer - despite the fact that PG personnel had prepared the underlying work. If that offer proves problematic, it is unclear whether PG or LD (or both) would be liable and, more importantly,
whose insurer would be on risk. That ambiguity creates risk for both firms and undermines the clarity of the delegation framework set out in the Pan-NOx AA. 



 



This is precisely why the Pan-NOx AA structured delegation at the firm level: to avoid splitting supervision and risk in a way that confuses accountability. The SL AA
 unpicks that structure and introduces unnecessary exposure. 



 



We refer you to 17(a) of the PTR skeleton argument filed by Mercedes where the Defendants have drawn the Court’s attention to this issue. 



 


4.                  
Client Consent 


If PG wishes for us and other PG staff to be instructed by, and report solely to, a firm other than PG, then this requires our express consent, and (we believe) the informed
 consent of the clients whom we act on behalf of (which will not only be just the clients of PG, but  may extent to all clients within every GLO if the work is to be Pan-NOx). If PG personnel are to carry out work on those clients’ cases under the direction
 of a different firm, the clients must be told who is supervising that work and must provide informed instructions to that effect. We refer you to Rule 1.4 of the Code of Conduct, which requires solicitors to ensure clients are in a position to make informed
 decisions about their representation. You cannot unilaterally impose this on us, or on any of the PG staff, nor PG’s clients as your email  suggests you can. 
 
You cannot unilaterally impose a change of supervisory firm on your employees or on the clients, as your email equally suggests. The assumption that this arrangement can simply be implemented without individual or client-level engagement is not supported by
 the regulatory framework. This concern is not novel: post our comments in this regard, this is also expressly identified in the skeleton argument filed by Mercedes at paragraph 17(b), where they raise the potential for regulatory impropriety in precisely these
 circumstances. 



Turning to other points specifically raised in your email:

You note that we are obliged to work our notice periods. Thank you for pointing this out again, although we note it is not consistent with representations that PG has
 made to the Defendants and Court that the timing of our last days are subject to ongoing discussion. You go on to say that once our notice period has expired, we are free to commence working for JLG, should we so choose. Collectively, none of us have informed

You have advised that LD and counsel have approved this solution. Please provide us with this correspondence (including the advice the firm has taken from counsel

 In circumstances where LD are waiting for PG to “sort out these issues with the team” and that they will “await the outcome”, we fail to understand how LD have approved the solution. 

 

·               
You advise that you are “now interviewing so with time this work-stream will be handed over”. Please explain which work-stream? Does this relate to non-common
 work? 


We repeat that we are keen to try and work together to find a collaborative solution to these issues, not least because of the importance of the upcoming PDD Trial beginning
 in a little over a week’s time and for which we are all deeply invested in and, in truth, where all of this is causing a huge and detrimental distraction. However, it is plain to us that the SL AA is plainly more than a simple delegation mechanism. It alters
 the control and supervision structure, restricts PG’s governance over its own staff, creates clear tension with employment contracts and regulatory obligations, and places work done on behalf of the PG clients under the instruction of an external law firm
 (without any proposal for client consent to be obtained). If there is to be a material change, it needs to be handled transparently and within a proper legal framework. We raise these points constructively and in good faith, with the shared goal of ensuring
 compliance and continuing to act in our clients’ best interests. 



We trust these concerns now demonstrate that the issues raised in the draft SL AA document need to be engaged with, and we look forward to hearing from you on those issues and

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you,
 as I’m sure you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we
 are. What is important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting
 my notice demonstrates that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation,
 I'm more than happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm;
 and ii) to address on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure
 the clients are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to
 those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall
 Pan-NOx CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for
 permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs,
 is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are
 not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications
 / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as
 it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date
 that will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical
 part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms
 as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it
 would appear the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale
 of importance considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe,
 will have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious
 link is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a
 professional and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is
 in the clients best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance
 with my professional and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to
 this. As such, I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings
 into the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then
 claim back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be
 in the employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where
 the firm has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial.
 This rental starts on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead
 booking me into hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and
 the recover the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.


Best,


Michael
